newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - After Moscow decree, holiday season starts early.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - After Moscow decree, holiday season starts early.

text.p: Santa Claus looked across the many holiday displays in Russia's most famous department store and complained about the ever-lengthening festive season.

"Unfortunately, we're already getting used to European Christmas on December 25, and then we have New Year and then (Orthodox) Christmas again on January 7," said Filip Kalabin, who doubles as Santa at the GUM Department Store on Red Square. "It's all driven by commerce."
Santa, called Father Frost in Russia, has had more work than ever this year.

Fuelled by business interest and the city authorities' desire to foster holiday cheer during the often-dreary month of December, Moscow's 1996 Christmas and New Year's holiday season has been officially extended.

Mayor Yury Luzkhov, parting with Moscow tradition in which stores decorate their windows after December 15, this year ordered Christmas trees, silver streamers, wreaths and other store decorations be in place by December 1.
Inspectors combed Moscow to ensure compliance.

"In Europe there is a long tradition of self-regulation by the market. Here we have to control certain things," said Lyudmila Ushakova, head of the Moscow Department of Consumer Affairs' information department. "It was decided if the holiday decorations came earlier, it would be pleasing to people."
A SOVIET HOLIDAY TWIST

Some stores are still fumbling with the idea of fusing holiday cheer and commerce. At Florens, a centrally located furniture store, an uninspiring collection of balloons, trees and lights are all that fill the 15-metre (50 feet) long window.

"We've decorated the window because of the mayor's order," said director Valery Bashkova, a fur coat draped across her legs. "Anyway, people can tell this is a furniture store -- it is written on the door."
Small artificial Christmas trees in the windows also tell visitors on Old Arbat street little about Savings Bank #7, another institution required to recast its usually grey facade.
"A bank is a solid organisation, so we'd like to have a more modest window display," said branch manager Marina Shikhina. "After all, we're not a store."
Even some city-sponsored efforts to spread good cheer suggest the heavy-handed Soviet past.
"The prefect of the central administrative district wishes you a Happy New Year!" reads one poster distributed to stores.

The Russian winter also conspires against a cheery holiday season. With the sun a rare visitor this December and the grey fading into darkness soon after 4 p.m., coloured blinking lights in city windows are having only a modest illuminating effect.
HOLIDAY CASH REGISTERS JINGLE
But many stores in the Russian capital are beginning to realise the benefits of exploiting the holiday spirit.
"If you see decorations everywhere, you remember that you must buy gifts," said Valentina Chechmeneva, administrator at the festive New Arbat food and household goods store.
A pioneer in creating holiday cheer has been the privatised State Department Store or GUM, a collection of individual stores inside cavernous 19th-century halls.
"Last year we learned that people are ready to buy early, and if we set up holiday displays first, we will win their business," said Irina Nikolayeva, head of GUM's team of window designers.
This strategy means that GUM now starts the holiday season -- which in Russia centres on the New Year and the Russian Orthodox Christmas on January 7 -- on November 25.
The date is so early that the store has ended its tradition of erecting a real Christmas tree inside and now uses a long-lasting artifical pine.
By city decree, it will be hard to buy a real tree for the home until December 20th, after which date the mayor has decided to allow tree markets to set up shop.
THE STONE AGE IS OVER
A few stores are also setting up display windows to appeal to those celebrating Christmas on December 25.
"We have decided to revive some old themes," GUM's Nikolayeva said as she pointed to a painting of the baby Jesus in a Red Square window. "We copied this image from a pre-revolutionary postcard."
Another sign of the changing times is a staple of the American Christmas, the holiday sale. Jewellery Store 9 is advertising holiday discounts of up to 30 percent, a first.
"It's to attract buyers. Before there were few jewellery stores but now we have many competitors," said store director Violetta Zhikina. "We are not in the Stone Age any more."
